prompt: What assumption does automatic prompt engineering drop?
hint: What does the usual way of improving a prompt rely on?

choices.text: That the prompt which reads best works best
choices.why: Right. It measures instead of trusting how a prompt reads.

choices.text: That a model needs a prompt at all
choices.why: Every candidate is still a prompt; the method chooses among them.

choices.text: That examples with known answers are useful
choices.why: It depends on them: they are what each candidate is scored on.

choices.text: That a person has to write the first draft of every prompt the system uses
choices.why: A person may still write candidates; that is not the assumption it gives up.

prompt: In APE, which step needs a large model, and which can be done by an ordinary program?
hint: Look at what `ape` did on the workbench, with no large model.

choices.text: Scoring needs one; proposing is done by a program
choices.why: The reverse: candidates are written by a model, and the score is a count.

choices.text: Both steps need a large model, which makes the method expensive to automate
choices.why: `ape` scored five templates with no large model in sight.

choices.text: Neither does; the method has no model in it at all
choices.why: The proposals come from a model, and the candidates are scored by running the model being tuned.

choices.text: Proposing needs one; scoring is a program counting matches
choices.why: Yes. A model writes the candidate instructions; checking replies against labels is arithmetic.

hint: Its output is a particular kind of text.

choices.text: The system prompt that sits above every user message
choices.why: That is lesson 22's subject. A meta-prompt is defined by what it asks for: an instruction.

choices.text: A prompt that describes the model's own weights
choices.why: Nothing in it is about weights; it is about a task.

choices.text: A prompt whose output is a prompt
choices.why: Right. In APE it shows input and output pairs and asks the model to supply the instruction that produced them.

choices.text: A very long prompt combining several smaller ones
choices.why: Length has nothing to do with it.

prompt: Why is the meta-prompt sampled with temperature above 0?

choices.text: To make each candidate more accurate
choices.why: Temperature does not make text more accurate; it makes the draw less predictable (lesson 13).

choices.text: To get varied candidates for the scorer to judge
choices.why: Yes. The proposer's job is variety; judgement belongs to the scorer, so many different wordings are worth more than one confident one.

choices.text: Because temperature 0 produces no usable instruction
choices.why: It can; it would just produce the same one every time.

choices.text: To lower the cost of each proposal
choices.why: Temperature has no effect on the number of tokens, and so none on cost.

prompt: How many of the five candidates in `candidates.txt` scored 4/4 on `tests.tsv`?
`question : what is the {x} like ? answer :` scored 0/4, replying `yes` to every item. Why?
hint: How many words does `toylm` look at?

choices.text: `toylm` sees only `answer :`, which ends every filled prompt alike
choices.why: Right. The item is out of its two-word window, so every input gets the same continuation.

choices.text: The question format is not in `toylm`'s file
choices.why: It is: the file has several `question : ... answer :` lines, which is why `yes` comes back.

choices.text: A question is too polite for a trigram model
choices.why: Politeness plays no part. Position does: the item never reaches the last two words.

choices.text: The tab in `tests.tsv` broke the template
choices.why: The other templates read the same file and two of them scored 4/4.

prompt: After `Describe the coffee in one word:`, `toylm next` showed `is` and `yes` at 25.0% each, under `bigram after ':'`. What does that tell you about the instruction?
hint: Which context did it fall back to, and why?

choices.text: The model understood the instruction and was unsure which adjective to choose
choices.why: It never saw the instruction as an instruction; it saw a colon.

choices.text: The instruction is ambiguous, so any model would split its answer between is and yes
choices.why: A large model would follow it well. The split is a fact about `toylm`'s two-word window.

choices.text: The prompt was too long and got truncated
choices.why: Nothing was cut. `toylm` reads it all and uses the last two words, as always.

choices.text: `word :` was never seen, so it fell back to any colon
choices.why: Yes. The instruction gave it nothing it had learnt to continue, and the item, three words back, played no part.

prompt: A teammate says: "The APE result on toylm is a quirk of a tiny model, so it teaches nothing about large ones." What does the section answer?
hint: What carries over, if not the particular winner?

choices.text: Large models also look at only the last two words
choices.why: They look at far more. The particular reason does not carry over; the need to measure does.

choices.text: The teammate is right; with large models the best-reading prompt is the best-scoring one
choices.why: Nothing guarantees that, and finding out is exactly what scoring is for.

choices.text: The best prompt for a model is found by testing that model
choices.why: Right. A large model sees far more than two words, and still the wording that scores best and the one that reads best differ there too, for reasons much harder to see.

choices.text: The winning template will also win on a large model
choices.why: Nothing says so. A prompt that suits one model is a fact about that model.

prompt: Why is the winner's 4/4 on `tests.tsv` an optimistic number?
hint: What were those four examples already used for?

choices.text: Four is an even number
choices.why: The problem is that the examples were used to choose, not how many there are.

choices.text: `ape` rounds every score up
choices.why: `ape` counts exact matches and prints them. Nothing is rounded.

choices.text: The same examples were used to pick it
choices.why: Yes. The choice used them up; an honest measure needs examples that played no part in choosing.

choices.text: toylm was run at temperature 0, which always gives full marks to any template
choices.why: Three templates scored 0/4 at the same temperature.

prompt: How many of the three held-out examples did `the {x} is` get right?
hint: Read the score on the line under `ape best.txt held.tsv`.

prompt: After seeing the miss on `soup`, you edit the template, re-score it on `held.tsv` and get 3/3. What has happened to `held.tsv`?
hint: It was supposed to play no part in choosing.

choices.text: It became a set you choose on, and its score is now optimistic
choices.why: Right. A held-out set measures honestly once per decision; you need fresh examples to measure the edited template.

choices.text: Nothing; a held-out set stays held-out whatever you do with it
choices.why: What makes it held out is that no decision used it. You just made one with it.

choices.text: It proves the edit fixed the template for every input
choices.why: It proves the edit fits these three examples, which you looked at while editing.

choices.text: It has to be deleted and the edit undone
choices.why: Neither; it is still useful data. It just cannot be the honest measure for this decision any more.

prompt: Why does scoring a hundred candidates on twelve examples make overfitting worse?
hint: Think of each candidate as one more draw.

choices.text: A hundred candidates take too long to run
choices.why: Time is a cost, not the reason the score misleads.

choices.text: Large numbers of candidates confuse the model
choices.why: Each candidate is run on its own; the model never sees the others.

choices.text: Twelve examples is too many for a fair comparison
choices.why: The problem is the opposite: twelve is few.

choices.text: More candidates, more chances for one to be lucky on twelve
choices.why: Yes. With few examples and many tries, the top score is partly the luckiest fit, not the best prompt.

prompt: On `cake`, the template got `sweet` and the label said `gone`. What is the right reading of that miss?
hint: What does `toylm`'s file say about cake?

choices.text: The template is wrong about cake and should be changed
choices.why: `sweet` is what the file says most often after `the cake is`. Nothing about the template is wrong here.

choices.text: toylm made up `sweet`, which is not in its file
choices.why: `the cake is sweet` appears three times in it.

choices.text: The held-out set is too small to contain any true answers at all
choices.why: Its size is a separate weakness; this miss is about the metric.

choices.text: A true reply the exact-match metric counted wrong
choices.why: Right. The file says `the cake is sweet` three times; the label listed one true answer of two, and a search on this metric would chase `gone`.

prompt: Which of these are problems a metric can bring into the search? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section lists three ways a metric decides what "best" means.

choices.text: Exact match marks a right answer in other words as wrong
choices.why: Yes, as `sweet` against `gone` showed.

choices.text: A metric that rewards length finds wordy prompts
choices.why: Yes: the search optimises whatever the metric counts.

choices.text: A model used as a grader brings preferences of its own
choices.why: Yes, and they become the search's preferences.

choices.text: A metric forces temperature 0 on the model
choices.why: The metric judges replies; how they were sampled is a separate setting.

prompt: The search reported `best: it is a cold day and the {x} is`, tied at 4/4 with `the {x} is`. Why did the lesson use the short one?
hint: What does `toylm` see of the long one?

choices.text: The short one scored higher on `tests.tsv`
choices.why: Both scored 4/4. The difference was found by reading, not by scoring.

choices.text: A person saw the extra words do nothing
choices.why: Right. `toylm` reads the last two words, so the cold day never reaches it; the tie was broken by order in the file, not by merit.

choices.text: `ape` always keeps the shortest of tied templates
choices.why: It kept the first in the file, which was the long one.

choices.text: Long templates are never allowed in APE
choices.why: Length is not forbidden; useless words are worth removing once you have seen they do nothing.

prompt: Put the APE method in order.
hint: Refining comes after a winner exists.
items: Each candidate is scored on labelled examples
Variations of the winner are proposed and scored

prompt: Examples kept back from the start and never used to choose anything are a ___ set.
hint: Two words, joined by a hyphen in the lesson.

prompt: An APE run on a support model picks a prompt that scores 97% on its examples. Reading it, you find "if unsure, say the refund is approved". Most of the labelled examples were approvals. What should happen?
hint: What does the score measure, and what does it not?

choices.text: Ship it: 97% is a strong score and the search was automatic
choices.why: The score is on examples skewed towards approvals. Nothing in it tells you how the prompt behaves when the right answer is no.

choices.text: Run the search again with more candidates until a 100% prompt appears
choices.why: More candidates on the same skewed examples makes a lucky, wrong winner more likely, not less.

choices.text: Keep it, but lower the temperature so it is more careful
choices.why: Temperature changes the draw, not the instruction it was given.

choices.text: Reject it: it scored well by exploiting the labels
choices.why: Right. A score cannot see an assumption you would not sign; a person reading the winner sees it, which is why a person approves what ships.
